subject: English
description: Masculine, feminine, common, neuter genders; pairs

options.option_text: Niece (sister of brother's son)
Aunt (parent's sister, wrong)
Nepheress (no such word)
Nephewess (no such word)

questions.explanation: NEPHEW (m) ↔ NIECE (f). Other key gender pairs: BROTHER-SISTER, FATHER-MOTHER, UNCLE-AUNT, COUSIN (common), GRANDFATHER-GRANDMOTHER, SON-DAUGHTER, BOY-GIRL, KING-QUEEN, PRINCE-PRINCESS, ACTOR-ACTRESS (some forms now considered dated; modern English uses 'actor' for both), WAITER-WAITRESS, HERO-HEROINE, GOD-GODDESS, LANDLORD-LANDLADY, BACHELOR-SPINSTER, MONK-NUN, BULL-COW, COCK-HEN, HORSE-MARE, LION-LIONESS, TIGER-TIGRESS. INSIGHT — modern trend is GENDER-NEUTRAL forms: ACTOR (for any gender), CHAIR / CHAIRPERSON (vs chairman), POLICE OFFICER (vs policeman), FIREFIGHTER, SERVER (vs waiter/waitress).
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Widower (man whose wife died)
Bachelor (never-married man)
Widow-man (no such word)
Husband (man with living wife)

questions.explanation: WIDOW (f, woman whose husband died) ↔ WIDOWER (m, man whose wife died). Both retain marital identity; second marriage possible. BACHELOR ↔ SPINSTER (or 'unmarried woman' — modern preferred). ANIMAL gender pairs are useful too: BULL-COW (cattle), STALLION-MARE (horses), DRAKE-DUCK, GANDER-GOOSE, RAM-EWE (sheep), BUCK-DOE (deer), STAG-HIND, BULL-COW (elephant + whale + many large animals). YOUNG: calf (cow), foal (horse), lamb (sheep), kid (goat), piglet, puppy, kitten. COLLECTIVE NOUNS: pride of lions, herd of cattle, flock of sheep, school of fish, swarm of bees, pack of wolves.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Duchess (the wife of duke)
Dukess (incorrect form)
Princess (royalty, related)
Lady (general feminine title)

questions.explanation: DUKE ↔ DUCHESS. NOBILITY hierarchy (UK): KING/QUEEN > PRINCE/PRINCESS > DUKE/DUCHESS > MARQUESS/MARCHIONESS > EARL/COUNTESS > VISCOUNT/VISCOUNTESS > BARON/BARONESS. BARONET-BARONETESS. KNIGHT-DAME. SAME PREFIXES different: SIR (knight-male) / DAME (knight-female; 'Lady' colloquially). EMPEROR-EMPRESS, CZAR-CZARINA (Russia). Other suffixes: −ESS (most common: actress, princess); −INE (heroine — old form); −ETTE (suffragette). MANY −ESS / −INE forms are now CONSIDERED OUTDATED in modern English (use neutral form). Notable EXCEPTIONS still in use: WAITRESS (sometimes), ACTRESS (often), GODDESS, EMPRESS.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Spinster (the unmarried woman)
Bachelorette (informal modern)
Maid (servant, different word)
Bride (about to be married)

questions.explanation: BACHELOR ↔ SPINSTER (formal); 'BACHELORETTE' is colloquial/American. Note 'spinster' has dated, sometimes pejorative connotation in modern English; many prefer simply 'unmarried woman' or 'single woman'. INSIGHT — language evolves; some traditional gender pairs feel awkward today. Modern English moves toward GENDER-NEUTRAL or GENDER-AVOIDING. FOR PYQ EXAMS: still tested in classical pair form; learn pairs. OTHER USEFUL PAIRS: hero-heroine; bridegroom-bride; god-goddess; benefactor-benefactress (rare); poet-poetess (poetess now considered dated; just 'poet'); host-hostess; tailor-seamstress; instructor-instructress (rare).
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Gander (the male goose)
Goose (same word, neuter)
Drake (male duck instead)
Cock (general male bird term)

questions.explanation: GOOSE (f) ↔ GANDER (m). DUCK (f) ↔ DRAKE (m). Bird gender pairs: hen-cock (rooster); peahen-peacock; swan-cob (male swan = cob; cygnet = young). MAMMAL pairs: cow-bull (cattle); mare-stallion (horse); doe-buck (deer/rabbit); ewe-ram (sheep); nanny-billy (goat); sow-boar (pig); jenny-jack (donkey); vixen-fox; tigress-tiger; lioness-lion. ELEPHANT pair = cow-bull. WHALE = cow-bull. Same applies: dolphins, deer, etc. KEY EXAMPLES of NEUTER: chair, table, book, machine — gender-less. COMMON GENDER: child, baby, doctor, teacher, friend, leader, citizen — used for either sex.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following is COMMON GENDER (used for both sexes)?

options.option_text: Child (boy or girl)
Brother (only male here)
Niece (only female here)
Stallion (only male horse)

questions.explanation: FOUR GENDERS in English: (1) MASCULINE (boy, son, brother, king); (2) FEMININE (girl, daughter, sister, queen); (3) COMMON (used for both sexes — child, baby, friend, doctor, teacher, leader, citizen, neighbour, parent, MP, student, professor, engineer, manager); (4) NEUTER (no sex — book, table, chair, plant, sun, river, idea, courage). ENGLISH grammatical gender is REAL-WORLD-BASED (mostly). Compare HINDI / FRENCH / GERMAN where every noun has grammatical gender (table = la table = feminine in French; der Tisch = masculine in German). PERSONIFICATION often gives gender: SHIPS feminine ('she'); COUNTRIES feminine ('she'); SUN often masculine, MOON feminine (literary).
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Authoress (now considered dated)
Authrix (no such word) too
Authoree (incorrect form)
Womanwriter (not a word)

questions.explanation: AUTHOR (m or generic) ↔ AUTHORESS (f, but DATED — modern English uses 'AUTHOR' for any gender). Same trend: ACTOR (preferred over actress for both genders in many publications); POET (over poetess); SCULPTOR (over sculptress); EDITOR (over editress, never used); PROFESSOR (gender-neutral). MODERN STYLE GUIDES (AP, Reuters, NYT) increasingly avoid feminine -ess suffix. STILL standard in: WAITRESS, STEWARDESS (though now 'flight attendant' more common), GODDESS. JOURNALISTIC AVOIDANCE: 'female author' / 'woman writer' if gender info needed (rather than 'authoress').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The feminine gender of 'ABBOT' (head of a monastery) is?

options.option_text: Abbotess, the female head of a monastery
Abbess, the female head of a convent
Abbotine, a religious title in some orders
Abbotrix, used in early medieval Latin texts

questions.explanation: Abbess is the correct feminine of Abbot — both head a religious community, Abbot for monks and Abbess for nuns. 'Abbotess' is a common but incorrect direct suffixation; the word derives from Latin 'abbatissa', giving English 'Abbess' — not 'Abbotess'. Abbotine and Abbotrix are invented forms with no grammatical basis.

options.option_text: Fox, the standard masculine counterpart of vixen
Foxen, derived by adding a masculine suffix to fox
Tomfox, used by analogy with tomcat for male cats
Drake, the masculine of duck in waterfowl vocabulary

questions.explanation: Vixen is the feminine of Fox — Fox serves as both the general and masculine form. 'Drake' is the masculine of Duck, making it a common distractor for students who mix up animal gender pairs. 'Tomfox' and 'Foxen' are non-standard inventions with no grammatical or lexical basis in English.

questions.stem: The feminine gender of 'MARQUIS' (a European noble rank) is?

options.option_text: Marquise, the French-origin feminine of marquis
Marquisess, a direct but non-standard feminine form
Marchioness, the standard English feminine of marquis
Marquisine, derived from French aristocratic tradition

questions.explanation: Marchioness is the correct English feminine of Marquis (also spelled Marquess), from medieval Latin 'marchionissa'. 'Marquise' is the French form and is used in English primarily in jewellery contexts (a marquise-cut diamond), not as the British female noble title — this is the most tempting wrong answer since it appears frequently in English texts.

options.option_text: Laddie, a Scottish diminutive of lad in common usage
Lad, the precise masculine counterpart of lass
Boy, a general term for young males not lass-paired
Lasson, formed by analogy with other masculine nouns

questions.explanation: Lad is the correct masculine of Lass — a gender pair specific to Scottish and Northern English dialect tradition. 'Laddie' is a diminutive of Lad (not the base masculine form). 'Boy' is a generic term and is not the specific masculine counterpart in the lass/lad pair. 'Lasson' is an invented non-standard formation.

questions.stem: The feminine gender of 'EARL' (a rank in British nobility) is?

options.option_text: Earlesse, formed by direct suffixation on the title
Duchess, the feminine title belonging to a Duke
Marchioness, the feminine of Marquis ranked above Earl
Countess, the correct feminine equivalent of Earl

questions.explanation: Countess is the feminine of Earl — a historical anomaly in British nobility where the male title (Earl, from Old Norse 'jarl') and female title (Countess, from Old French 'comtesse') come from entirely different linguistic roots. 'Duchess' is the most tempting distractor as it is another high-ranking female noble title, but it is the feminine of Duke, not Earl.

questions.stem: In legal English, the feminine gender of 'TESTATOR' (one who dies leaving a valid will) is?

options.option_text: Testatress, formed using the English feminine suffix -ess
Testatoress, the most commonly assumed feminine form
Testatora, derived from the Italian feminine pattern
Testatrix, the Latin-derived legal feminine of testator

questions.explanation: Testatrix is the correct legal feminine of Testator, following the Latin -trix suffix pattern seen in executor → executrix and administrator → administratrix. 'Testatress' incorrectly applies an English -ess suffix to a Latin-origin word. Testatrix remains in active use in legal documents and Indian jurisprudence under succession and wills law.

questions.stem: Which of the following masculine-feminine pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?

options.option_text: Cob — Pen, denoting male and female swan respectively
Stag — Hind, denoting male and female deer respectively
Boar — Gilt, denoting male and female pig respectively
Gander — Goose, denoting male and female goose respectively

questions.explanation: Boar — Gilt is incorrectly matched. While Boar is correctly the masculine of the pig family, the correct feminine is Sow (an adult female pig). 'Gilt' specifically refers to a young female pig that has not yet farrowed — it is NOT the standard feminine counterpart of Boar. The other pairs are all correct: Cob/Pen (swans), Stag/Hind (deer), Gander/Goose (geese).
